A key implication is that if reserve demand depends on the difference between current and expected future interest rates, but not on the current level per se, then the central bank can alter the market-clearing interest rate with no change in reserve supply. This implication is borne out in structural estimates of daily reserve demand and supply in the U.S.: expected future interest rates shift banks' reserve demand, while changes in the interest rate target are associated with no discernable change in reserve supply. The chapter concludes with a discussion of the implementation of monetary policy during the recent financial crisis, and the conditions under which the interest rate and the size of the central bank's balance sheet could function as two independent policy instruments. - Copy CitationBenjamin M. passages.text: Implementation of Monetary Policy: How Do Central Banks Set Interest Rates? Central banks no longer set the short-term interest rates that they use for monetary policy purposes by manipulating the supply of banking system reserves, as in conventional economics textbooks; today this process involves little or no variation in the supply of central bank liabilities. In effect, the announcement effect has displaced the liquidity effect as the fulcrum of monetary policy implementation. The chapter begins with an exposition of the traditional view of the implementation of monetary policy, and an assessment of the relationship between the quantity of reserves, appropriately defined, and the level of short-term interest rates. Event studies show no relationship between the two for the United States, the Euro-system, or Japan. Structural estimates of banks' reserve demand, at a frequency corresponding to the required reserve maintenance period, show no interest elasticity for the U.S. or the Euro-system (but some elasticity for Japan). passages.text: When the RBI Governor reads out "the repo rate stands at 5.25%", it sounds like a command. It is not. The Reserve Bank cannot phone SBI and order it to charge you 8% on a home loan. So how does one institution set the price of money for an entire economy of 1.4 billion people? The answer is a clever piece of plumbing: the central bank fixes a few key prices, builds a corridor around them, and then manages the quantity of money in the banking system to keep the market pinned where it wants. This guide explains how central banks set interest rates - the mechanics, the tools, and how it reaches you. Chapter 1 A central bank sets one price, not all prices The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) does not set the rate on your loan or your fixed deposit directly. It sets the rate at which it deals with commercial banks, and lets the market do the rest. The headline lever is the repo rate - the rate at which the RBI lends overnight money to banks against government securities (ClearTax). As of June 2026 it is 5.25%. Chapter 8 The science, the math and the art The science is monetary economics: the corridor system, liquidity management and inflation targeting are decades of refined theory and global practice. The math is the arithmetic of liquidity - how a CRR change of one percentage point releases or locks up tens of thousands of crores, and how the money multiplier amplifies it. The art is judgment: forecasting inflation a year ahead with messy data, then deciding how much growth to sacrifice for price stability. When banks are short of cash, the RBI lends to them (repo); when they are flush, it absorbs the excess (via the SDF). Calibrating these keeps the overnight rate near the repo rate. 3. Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR). Every bank must park a slice of its deposits with the RBI as cash, earning nothing. As of June 2026 the CRR is 3.00%. Raising it locks up money and tightens the system; cutting it releases money. It is a powerful, blunt tool used sparingly. 4. Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR). Banks must hold a minimum share of deposits in safe assets like government securities - 18.00% as of June 2026. It is more a prudential safety rule than a day-to-day rate tool, but it shapes how much banks can lend. 5. Forward guidance and stance. Sometimes the most powerful tool is words. By declaring a stance - "accommodative", "neutral", or "withdrawal of accommodation" - and signalling where rates may head, the RBI shapes expectations across the economy before it moves a single rupee. Their mandate is legally fixed: keep CPI inflation at 4%, within a 2% to 6% band. Everything else - growth, jobs, the rupee - is weighed, but price stability is the anchor. At the June 2026 meeting the MPC held at 5.25% with a neutral stance, judging that inflation, though currently soft, could drift toward the upper band on energy and weather risks. The published vote and minutes let the public see exactly who argued for what. Chapter 4 The toolkit: how the rate is actually enforced Setting a number is the easy part. Holding the market at that number takes active management of how much cash sloshes through the banking system - the system's liquidity. The RBI has several tools: 1. Open Market Operations (OMO). The RBI buys or sells government bonds. Buying bonds pushes cash into the banking system (softening rates); selling bonds drains cash out (firming rates). This is the day-to-day workhorse. 2. Chapter 5 From the decision to your bank Setting the rate is only half the battle; it must transmit to you. Most new Indian home loans are now tied to an external benchmark - usually the repo rate itself (a Repo-Linked Lending Rate). So when the MPC moves repo, these loans reset within a quarter. Older loans on internal benchmarks move more slowly and reluctantly. Deposit rates follow too, with banks cutting FD rates after a repo cut because they no longer need to compete as hard for your money. This is why the same MPC decision can feel fast or slow depending on your loan type - a recurring theme we cover in our transmission-mechanism guide. Because every bank can borrow from the RBI at this rate, no bank will lend to anyone else for much less or pay you much more than this benchmark allows. It becomes the anchor for the whole rate structure. The corridor: a floor and a ceiling The RBI does not just set one number floating in space. It builds a corridor so the overnight money-market rate cannot wander far: | Tool (June 2026) | Rate | What it does | |---|---|---| | MSF (Marginal Standing Facility) | 5.50% | Ceiling: a bank short of cash can always borrow here, so market rates rarely rise above it | | Repo rate | 5.25% | The policy signal, sitting in the middle | | SDF (Standing Deposit Facility) | 5.00% | Floor: a bank with spare cash can always park it here, so rates rarely fall below it | Source: codeforbanks, 5 June 2026. Here is the cascade you should expect: - The corridor slides down: SDF to about 4.50%, MSF to about 5.00%. - Overnight money-market rates fall toward 4.75%. - The RBI may add liquidity via OMO bond purchases to reinforce the cut. - Within a quarter, repo-linked home loans reset lower - a ₹50 lakh, 20-year loan sees its EMI fall by roughly ₹1,500 per month for each 0.50% cut. - FD and savings rates drift down over the following months. Read that way, a policy statement stops being noise and becomes a forecast of your own EMI and FD returns. Chapter 7 What this means for an ordinary saver You cannot vote on the MPC, but you can position for its decisions: - Watch the stance, not just the number. "Accommodative" hints at cuts ahead (good for borrowers, plan around falling FD returns); "withdrawal of accommodation" hints at hikes (lock FDs longer, brace for steeper EMIs). - Know your loan benchmark. Since April 2022, the RBI has used the SDF (rather than the old reverse repo) as its main tool to absorb surplus cash; it does not even require collateral. The logic of the corridor is elegant: no bank will lend to another for less than it can earn risk-free at the RBI's floor, and none will pay another bank more than it would cost to borrow from the RBI's ceiling. The overnight rate is trapped in between, and the repo rate in the middle is the dial the MPC turns. Chapter 3 Who actually decides: the MPC The repo rate is not the Governor's personal call. It is set by a six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC): three RBI officials and three external members nominated by the government. They meet roughly every two months, debate the data, and vote. Decisions go by majority, with the Governor holding a casting vote in a tie (Wikipedia: MPC). Their mandate is legally fixed: keep CPI inflation at 4%, within a 2% to 6% band.
